name: Just-be-her-type theory

card.summary: A dating-framework claim that attraction depends mainly on whether a man matches a particular woman's personal type, so that presenting and positioning yourself toward the type you fit is what raises your chances.
card.note: A community framework with no dedicated published research.

quick.overview:
The just-be-her-type theory holds that a woman's attraction is shaped chiefly by whether a man fits her individual preferences, her 'type', rather than by a universal ranking of looks.

For appearance, the implication proponents draw is that style, grooming and presentation can be tuned toward the type of woman one wants to attract, instead of chasing a single ideal. No published study has tested the theory as a whole.
quick.how: In practice, followers discuss identifying which features, styles or vibes tend to attract the people they are interested in and emphasising them through grooming, clothing and haircut.
quick.risks: The framework is a discussion-forum concept, not a clinical one, and carries no direct physical risk. Critics within the community argue that objective facial metrics matter more than type, which is the main counter-position.

lead: The just-be-her-type theory is a framework in looksmaxxing and dating discussions holding that a woman's attraction depends chiefly on whether a man matches her personal type, rather than on his position on a shared scale of attractiveness. People who use it to improve how they come across tailor hair, clothing, grooming and overall presentation toward the kind of partner they want to attract, instead of aiming at one universal ideal.[1]

The idea is usually set against the face-ranking approach in looksmaxxing, where features are scored on common scales such as the PSL rating and terms like mogging describe one person outshining another.[1] Followers of the type view say that a look that is unremarkable on such a scale can still be strongly preferred by people whose taste it fits.

No study has tested the theory under this name. Wider writing on attractiveness describes layers of shared taste, such as symmetry and youthfulness, alongside personal preferences that differ from person to person.[2]

chain: Identify the type of woman you want to attract
Tune grooming and style toward that type
Appear more appealing to people who share that type
angle.text: The framework suggests tailoring hair, clothing and grooming toward a target audience instead of one universal ideal. Followers see this as a way to stand out to people who prefer their look.

infobox: Attraction depends on matching a woman's personal type

paras: The theory treats a woman's type as a set of preferred traits, which may include build, hair, style, facial look and general vibe. Under the framework, a man is attractive to a given woman mostly to the degree that he resembles that type, so the same man can draw strong interest from some women and little from others.
Proponents present this as the reverse of the 'just be jacked' and face-metric frameworks, which place a single dominant trait at the top of a universal hierarchy.

In general terms, followers work out which looks, styles or aesthetics appeal to the group of people they are interested in and emphasise them through haircut, clothing, grooming and presentation. The approach is about positioning: choosing which cues to lean into rather than trying to raise every feature at once.

Reference summaries of attractiveness research describe three layers: perceptions shared across cultures, sociocultural norms, and individual preferences unique to each person.[2] The same summaries note large agreement among raters on which faces are attractive, which proponents of a type-based view and critics of it both draw on.[2]

The wider looksmaxxing movement is described in encyclopedic coverage as concerned mainly with traits such as height and facial structure, which the type theory sets aside in favour of individual fit.[1]

The theory appears as a counter-position in forum arguments over whether objective facial metrics or personal taste governs attraction. Community members who prioritise facial metrics argue that these matter more than type, and followers of the type view argue the reverse.

lore.intro: The theory circulates as forum shorthand in dating and looks discussions.[1]

claims.claim: Attraction depends mainly on whether a man matches a particular woman's type
claims.believers: Proponents hold that individual taste outweighs any universal ranking, so presentation aimed at a specific type raises appeal for those who share it.
claims.experts: Reference summaries describe both shared standards of attractiveness and personal preferences, and no published study has tested the claim as stated.[2]
